title: Death
lead: The Bible faces death plainly: humans are dust and return to dust. Genesis ties death to the first sin, and Paul says death came into the world through sin; other books speak of it as the common lot of all flesh. The older books mourn death and see Sheol as the end of striving; later books hope for resurrection; the New Testament calls death the last enemy, defeated by Christ.

sections.b: God warns that "on the day you eat from it you will die, yes die" (Genesis 2:17), and after the first sin, "For you are dust, / and to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19). "The days of our years add up to seventy, / or eighty for the strong" (Psalm 90:10). Ecclesiastes sees all go "back to the dust" (Ecclesiastes 3:20), and Ben Sira calls death "the Lord's sentence on all flesh" (Sirach 41:4). The place of the dead is Sheol (see that page). Daniel looks beyond it: many "will wake up" (Daniel 12:2). Paul teaches that "death through sin" passed to all people (Romans 5:12), that "The last enemy to be brought to an end is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Hebrews says Christ set free "all who lived their whole lives as slaves because they were afraid to die" (Hebrews 2:15). In the new creation "Death will be gone" (Revelation 21:4).

sections.h: Death as sentence, as lot, and as enemy
sections.b: The books do not all speak of death in the same terms. In Genesis it is the sentence on the first sin (Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:19), and Paul builds on that: "death through sin" passed to all people (Romans 5:12). Ecclesiastes speaks of it as the one fate humans share with animals: "they share one fate" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). Ben Sira calls it "the Lord's sentence on all flesh" (Sirach 41:4), to be accepted without fear, and says nothing of sin there. The New Testament treats it as an enemy that Christ defeats (1 Corinthians 15:26). See also the pages on Sheol, resurrection, the fall and the intermediate state.
